explanations.answer: Absalom will overtake them and strike the city
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. David says Absalom, his son, “will soon overtake us, heap disaster on us, and put the city to the sword.” When a king says "we must leave quickly," he's not talking about beating traffic. The danger he names is Absalom catching up.

explanations.answer: The gates will be shut and they'll be trapped
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but David never says a word about gates. What he says is that Absalom “will soon overtake us, heap disaster on us, and put the city to the sword.” Nobody in this scene is locking anything. They're headed OUT, and fast.

explanations.answer: The people will turn on them in the streets
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd think it, since the messenger just said the hearts of the men of Israel are with Absalom. But that's not what David says will happen. His warning is about Absalom himself: “he will soon overtake us, heap disaster on us, and put the city to the sword.” He's watching the road behind him, not the street beside him.

Not quite, friend. The text says the opposite: “Then the king set out, and his entire household followed him.” Nobody in that house is staying home on the couch. The only ones left behind are ten concubines, who stay to take care of the palace.

That's right. “Then the king set out, and his entire household followed him.” That's the whole house on the move, no one left folding laundry. The only ones he leaves behind are ten concubines to take care of the palace.
Yes, baker, the palace. The text says David left behind ten concubines “to take care of the palace.” Everyone else in the household goes with him. It's a quiet detail in a very loud day.
Gates sounds official, like a job with a clipboard and a little hat. But the text says he left the ten concubines behind “to take care of the palace.” The gates aren't mentioned in that verse at all.
Fields would be a lot of walking for a day like this one. But the text says the ten concubines stay behind “to take care of the palace.” That's the one place David's household leaves covered.

explanations.answer: Wherever the king goes he will be there
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Ittai says, “wherever my lord the king may be, whether it means life or death, there will your servant be!” Remember, he's a foreigner who only showed up yesterday. I've had friends in a junk drawer who wouldn't have stuck around for THAT offer.

explanations.answer: He will go back and serve the new king
explanations.explanation: That's what David tells him to do, not what Ittai says. David says, “Go back and stay with the new king.” Ittai answers with a promise to stay: “wherever my lord the king may be, whether it means life or death, there will your servant be!” He doesn't take the exit.

explanations.answer: He will head home and wait for news
explanations.explanation: Ittai doesn't head anywhere but forward. Waiting for news is what David plans for himself at the fords of the wilderness. Ittai says, “wherever my lord the king may be, whether it means life or death, there will your servant be!” He's not waiting by any phone.

Yes, baker. After Ittai's promise, David says, “March on then,” and Ittai marches past with all his men and all the little ones who were with him. David gave the man a way out and he didn't take it. That's a whole crowd choosing to stay close.

It's actually true. David says, “March on then,” and the text says Ittai the Gittite marched past with all his men and all the little ones who were with him. Ittai had just promised to stay with the king, and this is him doing it. The little ones come along too.

Right on, baker. As the king crosses the Kidron Valley, “all the people also passed toward the way of the wilderness.” That's the direction of the whole crowd, not just David. Nobody's packing for a good time out there.

The city is what they're leaving, friend. The text says that as the king crossed the Kidron Valley, “all the people also passed toward the way of the wilderness.” Heading toward the city would be a U-turn, and nobody's doing one.
No beach day on this trip, baker. The text says they passed “toward the way of the wilderness,” after the king crossed the Kidron Valley. No sea is mentioned anywhere in the verse.

explanations.answer: The LORD will bring him back to see it again
explanations.explanation: That's it. David says, “If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, He will bring me back and let me see both it and His dwelling place again.” He's handing the whole matter to the LORD instead of holding on to the ark himself. I think that took a lot of trust.

explanations.answer: The LORD will send the ark out to him
explanations.explanation: David doesn't say the ark will come to him. He says the LORD “will bring me back and let me see both it and His dwelling place again.” The ark goes back to Jerusalem, and David is the one who hopes to return.

explanations.answer: The LORD will give him a new city
explanations.explanation: A new city isn't in this verse, baker. David says, “If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, He will bring me back and let me see both it and His dwelling place again.” His hope is the same old city with the ark in it.

explanations.answer: Let the LORD do whatever seems good to Him
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. David says, “But if He should say, ‘I do not delight in you,’ then here I am; let Him do to me whatever seems good to Him.” That's a king with nothing in his hands, putting himself in the LORD's. It's a hard sentence to say out loud.

explanations.answer: He will fight to take back his throne
explanations.explanation: That's not what David says in this verse. He says, “then here I am; let Him do to me whatever seems good to Him.” There's no battle plan in it, only a king standing there with open hands.

explanations.answer: He will leave Israel and never return
explanations.explanation: David doesn't announce any big exit here. He says, “then here I am; let Him do to me whatever seems good to Him.” "Here I am" is a man staying put and leaving the decision to the LORD.

explanations.answer: Word from Zadok in the city
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. David tells Zadok, the priest, “I will wait at the fords of the wilderness until word comes from you to inform me.” He sends the priests back to Jerusalem and plans to hear from them there. That's a lot of trust sent back down the road.

Ittai already marched past with all his men, so nothing in the text has him fetching more. David says he'll wait at the fords of the wilderness “until word comes from you to inform me.” That "you" is Zadok, the priest.

No peace offer is coming in this passage, baker. David says he will wait at the fords of the wilderness “until word comes from you to inform me.” He's talking to Zadok, the priest, and he's waiting on news from the city.

That's right. The text says, “all the people with him covered their heads and went up, weeping as they went.” David's head is covered, and so is everyone else's. This is a whole mountain of people walking up together.

It's actually true, baker. The text says, “all the people with him covered their heads and went up, weeping as they went.” David wasn't doing it alone. The whole line climbing the Mount of Olives looked just like him.

Yes, baker. Ahithophel is the counselor who is now among Absalom's conspirators, and David pleads, “O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness!” Notice where he takes it: straight to the LORD, while he's still walking up the hill. I think that's the quickest prayer on the whole mountain.

explanations.answer: Bring Ahithophel back to David's side
explanations.explanation: David doesn't ask for that here. He pleads, “O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness!” His request is about the advice Ahithophel gives, not about getting the man back.

explanations.answer: Let Ahithophel fall in the next battle
explanations.explanation: No battle comes up in this prayer, baker. David pleads, “O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness!” It's all about the advice, and nothing is said about Ahithophel falling.

That's it. David tells Hushai, “you can thwart the counsel of Ahithophel for me if you return to the city.” Hushai the Archite, David's friend, is being sent in as David's man on the inside. David has just asked the LORD to turn that counsel into foolishness, so this is a job on the same problem.

explanations.answer: To talk Absalom into giving up
explanations.explanation: Nothing in David's plan says Hushai will talk Absalom out of anything. David says, “you can thwart the counsel of Ahithophel for me if you return to the city.” The target is Ahithophel's advice.
The palace is where Hushai is sent, but guarding it isn't the job. David says, “you can thwart the counsel of Ahithophel for me if you return to the city.” This is more of a mission than a post.

It's the other way around, baker. David tells Hushai, “Report to them everything you hear from the king’s palace.” The "them" is Zadok and Abiathar, the priests. Hushai isn't keeping anything from them.

Right. David says, “Will not Zadok and Abiathar the priests be there with you? Report to them everything you hear from the king’s palace.” He wants Hushai telling the priests everything. That's a secret that's meant to travel.

You got it, baker. David says the priests' two sons, Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Jonathan son of Abiathar, are there with them, and tells Hushai, “Send them to me with everything you hear.” So the news goes from Hushai to the priests, then out with the two sons. That's a three-stop delivery route.

Ittai and his men are marching with David, not sitting in Jerusalem. The messengers are the priests' sons, as David says: “Send them to me with everything you hear.” He means Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Jonathan son of Abiathar.

The Cherethites and Pelethites marched past David on his way out of the city, so they're with him. The messengers are in Jerusalem with the priests: Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Jonathan son of Abiathar. David says, “Send them to me with everything you hear.”
